abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: During the evolution of vertebrates, significant transformations have occurred in the visual transmission and processing pathways. However, our understanding of the differences between two primary visual pathways in vertebrates and their evolutionary changes remains limited. The emerging technologies and comparative analysis have provided us with a more comprehensive way to decipher this process. Here, we applied single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) onto the avian optic tectum, one of the key visual subcortical hubs in birds, to construct its cellular landscape. By integrating these data with mammalian snRNA-seq datasets, we revealed differences in the density of two types of thalamic-projecting excitatory neurons within the retinotectal pathway of birds and mammals. Additionally, a series of shared molecules were identified between two types of dominant visual pathways in vertebrates. Overall, this work provides a novel focus on the evolution of visual pathways and establishes a framework for their comparative analysis.

list-item.p: snRNA-seq constructs the cellular landscape of avian tectum
Cross-hemispheric lateralization at the transcriptional level is subtle
Two distinct projecting neuron types are enriched in the retinotectal pathway
Thirteen functional molecules were shared across dominant visual pathways in vertebrates

abstract.p: Evolutionary developmental biology; Model organism; Ornithology; Transcriptomics

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Vision enables vertebrates to instantaneously perceive and understand their surroundings. Throughout the course of evolution, several remarkable changes have taken place in the visual systems of various species.1,2,3 Although extensive research has sought to unravel these processes, the evolution of visual perception and processing still remains a substantial enigma.

Currently, two primary pathways are involved in the vision of vertebrates: the retinotectal pathway and the retinogeniculate pathway (Figure 1A).3 In non-mammalian vertebrates, ascending visual signals are predominantly transmitted through the retinotectal pathway. For instance, birds, which have developed exceptional visual abilities among vertebrates, project approximately 90% of their retinal output to the tectum. From there, signals are transmitted to the entopallium of the dorsal ventricular ridge (DVR) via the thalamic nucleus rotundus (Rt).4,5 This transmission process is conserved in non-mammalian vertebrates, and it is also regarded as the major visual processing mode owned by the common ancestor of vertebrates.3 However, in mammals, this process has gradually shifted toward the predominant utilization of the retinogeniculate pathway.6 In humans, for example, the lateral geniculate nucleus (LG) in the thalamus, rather than the superior colliculus (SC, the homologous region of optic tectum [OT] in mammals), directly receives most retinal afferents.6 These signals are subsequently projected to the well-developed visual cortex in forebrain. Despite these advances in our understanding of the parallel visual pathways, the underlying molecular mechanism for this transition and the fundamental differences between these two visual pathways in vertebrates remain elusive.Figure 1
The single-nucleus resolution transcriptomic landscape of avian tectum

(B) Schematic diagram of the snRNA sequencing workflow for rock pigeons (Columba livia) and zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata).
(C) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plot showing snRNA data of avian OT from zebra finch (left) and pigeon (right). Exn, excitatory neurons; Inn, inhibitory neurons; Oli, oligodendrocytes; Ast, astrocytes; OPCs, dendrocyte precursor cells; Mic, microglial cells; VLMCs, vascular smooth muscle cells; Bld, blood cells.
(D) The correlation of major OT cell types between zebra finch and pigeon. ρ: Spearman correlation coefficient. ∗∗∗: p value < 0.001. ∗∗: p value < 0.01.
(E) UMAP plot showing the integration and re-clustering of neurons of two species.
(F) Gene expression patterns in the integrated snRNA-seq data, spatial transcriptome (ST) data of zebra finches, and in situ hybridization (ISH) results of zebra finch. SGC, stratum griseum centrale; SGF, stratum fibrosum periventriculare; Ipc, nucleus isthmi pars parvocellularis; SGP, stratum griseum periventriculare. Scale bar, 500 μm for ST and 1 mm for ISH.

As one of the major visual hubs in vertebrates, the OT/SC structure exhibits a relatively complex architecture and diverse functions. Previous studies have demonstrated its important role in various functions, including visual processing, eye movement, and multimodal sensory integration.7,8 Due to its direct connections with eyes, the OT/SC can rapidly receive and process external information, subsequently driving the motion of organisms. The rapid detection and response to visual threats are considerably critical for the survival of animals. Consequently, the role of OT/SC in fear response, particularly in rapid emergency avoidance when faced with dangers or predators, has been extensively studied and reported.9 Additionally, the OT/SC is also believed to be involved in some higher functions, such as selective attention, learning, and cognition.9,10,11 Therefore, compared with other subcortical visual hubs, the OT/SC is recognized as a brain region with more complicated functions.

Although the size and detailed structure of the OT/SC vary among different vertebrates, it remains one of the most conserved regions in the vertebrate brain, with a clear homologous relationship among species.9,12,13 The OT in non-mammal vertebrates and mammalian SC both possess a layered structure, and the complexity of OT has reached its peak in birds that have a region comprising about 15 detailed layers.12 Beyond macrostructural similarities, the generation of the visual map in the OT/SC is also considerably conserved among vertebrates. In most reported vertebrates, OT/SC forms and aligns the biological sensory map by its laminar architecture according to the topological structure of the surrounding environment.8 Comparatively, the research and attention on other subcortical visual hubs have been relatively limited. For example, to date, no definitive homologous region for the avian nucleus rotundus (Rt) has been identified in the mammalian thalamus, although some scholars propose it may be the pulvinar.8 Thereby, given the conserved nature and clear homologous relationship of the OT/SC across vertebrates, we selected it as a representative model to investigate the evolution of subcortical visual pathways in this study.

By applying single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and high-resolution spatial transcriptomic sequencing technologies in this study, we could obtain a more comprehensive cellular landscape of the avian OT. In our previous study,14 we focused on a subset of the OT regions, aiming to investigate the potential functional complexity within the deeper OT layers. In the current work here, we presented a new single-nuclei dataset covering the entire avian OT to examine the evolution and variation in visual processing, which is primarily mediated by the outer OT layers. This study involved new sampling and analyses specific to these areas, providing a more comprehensive dataset that will serve as a valuable resource and complement for studies on visual processing and midbrain organization in avian species. Furthermore, through the comparative analysis of different species and visual pathways here, we identified a series of cellular innovations and conservations that existed in the evolution of vertebrate vision.

sec.title: Single-nucleus transcriptional landscape of avian tectum
sec.p: As one of the main branches of vertebrate evolution, birds have played a crucial role in numerous visual research and cross-species comparisons. However, a comprehensive understanding of the cellular and molecular organization in the avian brain, particularly in some subcortical regions, is still lacking. Here, we focused on the tectum, a primary visual processing and transmission hub in the avian brain, and used snRNA-seq to reconstruct its systematic cellular architecture.

In order to acquire a more representative landscape of avian tectum, we included two representative avian species in this study: pigeons (Columba livia) and zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata), which possess different visual capabilities and distinct tectum volume (Figure 1B). After sequencing and stringent quality control (see STAR Methods), we obtained a total of 49,273 pigeon OT nuclei and 28,569 zebra finch OT nuclei (Figures 1C, S1A, and S1B). Referring to the unsupervised clustering results and expression of canonical marker genes, we manually annotated eight major cell types in avian tectum (Figures S1C and S1D). The major cell types in the two species included: the excitatory neurons (Exn), inhibitory neurons (Inn), oligodendrocytes (Oli), astrocytes (Ast), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), microglial cells (Mic), vascular smooth muscle cells (VLMCs), and blood cells (Bld). Through the transcriptional correlation among cell types, we substantiated the high conservation within the cellular composition of avian OT (Figure 1D).

After extracting and re-clustering neuronal cells from two species, we further categorized a total of 56,996 neurons into 18 distinct sub-groups (marked as clu0–clu17), highlighting the complex neuronal composition within avian OT (Figures 1E and S1E; Table S1). To further understand the architecture and functional mechanisms of avian OT, we examined the expression patterns of several essential molecules, which were reported previously, in our avian snRNA-seq data. Meanwhile, we checked the spatial distribution of these genes with our previous spatial transcriptome data and the in situ hybridization (ISH) data (Figure 1F).14,15

The CABP7 has been reported as a significant marker gene for the key visual signal output layer—the stratum griseum centrale (SGC)—within OT.12,14,16 Here, it was primarily expressed in the Exn population, especially in the clu14 group. We also verified the spatial enrichment of CABP7 expression in the SGC layer by the spatial transcriptome and ISH results (Figure 1F). OTX2 is one of the main markers for the OT superficial layers, which is involved in the main visual signal reception and processing of OT.12 It was found to be mainly expressed in inhibitory subtypes and distributed relatively uniformly in the outermost layers of the OT according to our spatial data (Figure 1F).

Several previous studies in mice have demonstrated that CBLN2+ neurons are the principal cell type projecting from the SC to the lateral posterior nucleus (LP) in the thalamus and mediate the escape from predators.17,18 In mice, these cells are mainly distributed in the superficial layers of the SC.18 Conversely, in the avian OT, we found the CBLN2+ neurons were mainly enriched in the nucleus isthmi pars parvocellularis (Ipc) (Figure 1F), which is an important visual processing nucleus in the deep layers of the avian OT and lacks homologous regions in mammals.19 This result preliminarily indicated the structural differences between avian OT and mammal SC in the thalamic projection and neuronal circuit related to innate escape reactions. Lastly, the CCK+ neurons have been reported to be involved in various complex life activities.20 Here, we found the expression of CCK in multiple OT Exn cell groups and identified its distribution around the stratum griseum periventriculare (SGP), which is a region processing multiple types of information and mediating motor functions in the avian OT.9

Collectively, here we provided a single-cell resolution atlas of avian OT, which could bring us a systematic insight into the avian midbrain cellular composition. Furthermore, we identified the expression patterns of several essential genes in our data and elucidated their spatial enrichment, which could reflect the functional and structural specialization of avian OT. Meanwhile, the identification of markers from the innermost to the outermost layers in the OT also well validated the comprehensive coverage of tissue sampling and cell capture in our snRNA-seq data (Figure 1F).

sec.title: Cross-hemispheric transcriptional lateralization of avian tectum
sec.p:
The OT/SC structure has been one of the most studied models for the topographic projection of neurons and selective axonal extension, as well as the axonal plasticity of the nervous system. In fishes and adult birds, there is virtually no ipsilateral visual projection from the retina to OT.21 However, in mammals, especially primates, the proportion of ipsilateral neural projections gradually increases and the binocular vision is fully developed (Figure 2A).22 Hence, the avian model here provided possibilities for further exploring the occurrence of this transition during vertebrate evolution. Additionally, compared with mammals, birds lack highly developed communication or interference structures, like corpus callosum, between two hemispheres.23,24 Therefore, compared to previous studies on lateralization of the left and right brain based on mammalian models, the avian model in this study offers advantages in excluding the interference of ipsilateral stimulates and cross-hemispheric information exchange, allowing for a more comprehensive evaluation of asymmetries between hemispheres.Figure 2
Cross-hemispheric gene expression difference in avian tectum
(A) Schematic highlighting the ratio of ipsilateral retinal projections among vertebrates.
(B) UMAP plot showing pigeon OT single-nucleus atlas grouped by right and left brain. OT – L, left OT. OT – R, right OT.
(C) Count of differentially upregulated genes cross left and right OT. DEGs with average log2(fold change) >0.25 and adjusted p value <0.05 were counted.
(D) Volcano plot showing DEGs of Exn (left), Inn (median), and Ast (right). avg_log2FC, average log2(fold change); p_val_adj, adjusted p value.
(E) Violin plot showing the expression patterns of selected DEGs among major cell types.
(F) Spatial expression level of certain DEGs in pigeon OT by spatial transcriptome data. D, dorsal; V, ventral. Scale bar, 1 mm.

In this study, we dissected and sequenced the left and right OT of our pigeon samples separately (Figures 1C and S2A), and found no significant hemispheric difference in their major cellular composition (Figures 2B and S2B). However, the number of hemisphere-specific expression genes (HEGs) varied among cell types (Figure 2C; Table S2). Overall, the Exn, Inn, and Ast showed the most remarkable asymmetries compared with other major cell types. We then focused on these three cell types and examined their HEGs. These HEGs were mainly enriched in pathways including cellular chemotaxis, axonal extension, neurodevelopment, and energy consumption (Figure S2C). For instance, the ephrin type-A receptor family, including EPHA3 and EPHA6, showed significant expression preference between the left and right OT (Figure 2D). EPHA3 regulates cellular morphology, adhesion, and migration in multiple biological processes and was implicated in mediating developmental events, particularly in the nervous system.25 Particularly, EPHA3 was reported to get involved in the retinotectal mapping of neurons and the correct axonal segregation in the brain.26,27 Moreover, it had been proven necessary in the stimulation for nasal retinal ganglion cell axon growth and the retinotectal topographic map formation of chicken.28 In this study, we found the EPHA6 seemed to have similar axonal guidance functions as the EPHA3 in the retinotectal visual system, which had previously been demonstrated only in the retina.29 In addition to EPHA3 and EPHA6, a series of neurodevelopment-related molecules, including ADGRL2, NR2F1, and SYT1, exhibited expression asymmetries that may contribute to well-balanced visual formation (Figure 2D).30,31,32,33 YWHAG, previously reported as a psychosis-related factor, also showed hemispheric preference in this study.34,35 As one of the classic marker genes of astrocytes, AQP4 plays an important role in supporting neurons of sensory hubs of the central nervous system (CNS),36 further highlighting the significance of astrocytes in the cross-hemispheric specialization (Figure 2D).

Benefitting from single-cell and spatial sequencing technologies, here we could further elucidate the cell type preference and spatial distribution of these HEGs. The HEGs between right and left OT were found to be cell-type-restricted (Figures 2E and S2D). For instance, the EPHA6 was enriched in Exn, whereas the EPHA3 presented higher expression in Inn and VLMCs. ADGRL2 showed a difference in neurons, while SYT1 exhibited divergence among Ast. Spatially, we found that HEGs primarily appeared in the superficial layers of the avian tectum, particularly in the stratum griseum fibrosum (SGF), which is the pivotal layer for visual signal input in the retinotectal pathway (Figure 2F).12,37 Notably, the HEGs from Ast, like SYT1 and NEFL, are also enriched in the Ipc. Overall, the spatial distribution patterns of these HEGs further demonstrated their close involvement in visual formation.

Collectively, here we revealed the HEGs of major cell types between the right and left avian tectum. As a non-model organism model, the avian OT showed a series of asymmetric molecules in the subcortical visual pathway, bringing new insights into the selective axonal extension of optic nerve fibers from the retina to OT/SC. Notably, in spite of the rare interaction between the avian two tectal hemispheres, our analysis only revealed a limited number of HEGs with relatively small expression fold change, similar to previous studies in mammals (Figures 2D and S2E).38,39 This may highlight that the difference between the left and right brains at the transcriptional level was limited. Presumably, as reported in previous studies, more fundamental cross-hemispheric differences may exist at other levels, such as intricate neural circuits in the CNS or the expression differences in dynamic situations.40

sec.title: Transformation of visual thalamic project weight in the retinotectal pathway of vertebrates
sec.p:
Two parallel visual pathways were broadly observed in the CNS of vertebrates; however, the fundamental differences and conservations across species are still elusive (Figure 1A). To further explore innovations in the retinotectal pathway among vertebrates, here we integrated the snRNA data of neurons from avian OT and human SC, representing two typical models of the visual weight shift during evolution (Figure S3A).41 Overall, the integration results revealed highly conserved cellular composition among avian OT and the human SC (Figure 3A). Additionally, using the same clustering parameters, we observed that the Inn were consistently more heterogeneous in the OT/SC structure compared to the Exn (Figures 1E and 3A).Figure 3
Integration and comparison of avian OT and human SC
(A) UMAP plot showing the integration of snRNA-seq data from birds and humans, colored by unsupervised clusters (left) and species (right).
(B) Feature plot of CABP7 and CBLN2 in integrated data of birds and humans.
(C) The CABP7+ cell proportion and CBLN2+ cell proportion among excitatory neurons of humans, mice, and birds. p, Kruskal-Wallis test.
(D) Volcano plot showing DEGs of cluster Exn4 between humans and birds. p_val_adj, adjusted p value; log2FC, log2(fold change).
(E) Spatial expression of SPHKAP and LRRK1 in zebra finch and pigeon. Scale bar, 50 μm for zebra finch and 1 mm for pigeon.
(F) Stack bar plot showing relative species proportion of all cell types. Clusters with certain species proportions larger than 0.75 were highlighted. The Inn10 was omitted for its cell number was less than 100.
(G) Heatmap showing the expression level of top 5 DEGs from Exn5, Inn1, and Inn9.
(H) Bubble plot showing compared GO enrichment results of DEGs from Exn5, Inn1, and Inn9.

Among these clusters, we mainly focused on the thalamic projection neurons and noticed a special population of Exn—the Exn4. In both birds and humans, the Exn4 were identified as a special group of thalamic projecting neurons based on the expression of canonical markers CABP7 and CBLN2, respectively (Figure 3B). Despite transcriptional similarities compared with other neuron types in the UMAP plot, these Exn4 cells exhibited distinct divergence with a contrary projecting pattern (Figures 3A and 3B). As described before, the CABP7+ Exn in birds mainly project to the Rt in the avian thalamus, conveying most visual information to higher visual centers and playing essential roles in avian visual sensing.12,14,16 We thus termed them vision-related projecting neurons to denote their primary functions in this study. On the contrary, in mammals, the CBLN2+ Exn seems more reflex-related, which project to the LP in mammalian thalamus, instead of the homologous region of Rt in mammals, and are mainly involved in innate escape reactions when facing dangers.17,18

In this study, we proposed that this transition from vision-related projecting neurons to the reflex-related might contribute to the diminishing portion of the retinotectal pathway in mammals, leaving the SC primarily involved in innate reactions instead of visual perception. To verify this assumption, we included another snRNA-seq dataset from mouse SC (Figure S3B).42 Focusing on the Exn groups, we found a significant gradient change in the proportion of CABP7+ Exn and CBLN2+ Exn in the OT/SC structure from birds to mice and humans, corresponding with the gradual weight shift observed in vertebrate evolution (Figure 3C). The avian OT exhibited the highest density of CABP7+ neurons, whereas in mammals, particularly in humans, we observed a higher proportion of excitatory neurons positive for CBLN2 in the SC. Accordingly, this coincidental finding preliminarily substantiated our hypothesis: different types of thalamic projecting neurons might contribute to the differential function execution and specification within the retinotectal pathway of vertebrates.

To further clarify potential molecular differences in these projecting neurons between birds and humans, we identified the differential expressed genes (DEGs) of Exn4 (Figure 3D and Table S3). We found some potassium channel-related molecules, like the KCNIP4 and KCTD16, were significantly upregulated in the human SC Exn4. Besides, the fibroblast growth factor 14 (FGF14) also presented a high expression level, which was reported to mediate the excitatory synapse development and axon initial segment.43,44 The leucine-rich repeat transmembrane neuronal 4 (LRRTM4) is a transsynaptic adhesion protein regulating glutamate synaptic assembly, which was proved to be a novel synapse arrangement regulator in retinal bipolar cells.44,45 It presented a cross-species expression difference in the OT/SC structure in this study and might contribute to the selective projection of the retinotectal pathway in vertebrates. Among the avian upregulated genes, some showed an obvious enrichment in the SGC, such as LRRK1 and SPHKAP, consistent with the expression pattern of CABP7, which could further demonstrate the vision-related functions of the avian Exn4 cells (Figures 1F and 3E).

Beyond the projecting neurons, to obtain a more comprehensive insight into innovations in the OT/SC structure, we compared the relative composition of all clusters. Three groups of neurons with striking different densities among birds and humans were identified here, which included the Exn5, Inn9, and Inn7 (Figure 3F). Most of the Exn5 and Inn9 cells were from avian OT, while the Inn7 showed a higher density in human SC. Notably, we found the Inn10 was unique to pigeons, so we omitted this group when further exploring the common differences between birds and humans (Figure S3C). In this study, we found that these species-related neuron types exhibited distinct transcriptional signatures in the OT/SC (Figure 3G; Table S4). The Exn5 was marked by SCN4B, CNNM2, and SLITRK4, while the Inn9 highly expressed CXCL14, SEMA3A, and SVEP1. For the human-enriched Inn1, GRIK4, KCNIP4, and DLGAP1 were significantly upregulated (Figure 3G). To evaluate the function of these cell populations, we conducted a compared gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis on their significantly upregulated DEGs (Figure 3H). The results indicated that the visual system development-related pathways primarily enriched in the bird-enriched Exn5 population, which is consistent with the stronger retinotectal vision capacity in birds. Spatially, we found Exn5 mainly distributed in the SGC, Ipc, and nucleus isthmi pars magnocellularis (Imc) regions (Figure S3D). These regions were essential functional domains of avian OT while processing the visual input and output, and their homologous areas in mammals still remain elusive.12,46 The Inn9 was found to be related with the response to fibroblast growth factors and regulation of axonogenesis, and it significantly enriched in the outmost SGF layer of the avian OT (Figures 3H and S3D). The SGF layer is the main region in OT receiving visual projection from retina and is significantly thickened in the birds.12 Thus, we speculated that the particular high abundance of Inn9 in birds might be related with the remarkable expansion of the avian OT compared to other vertebrates.

Together, through the cross-species comparison, we identified two different types of projecting Exn in the avian OT and mammalian SC. In birds, numerous vision-related Exn4 cells delivered the visual information from SGC to Rt and higher centers. Conversely, in humans, the reflex-related neurons dominated the thalamic projection. Among all neuron subtypes, most of them remained conservative, while three groups—Exn5, Inn1, and Inn9—exhibited species-specific differences. Exn5 and Inn9 appeared to be associated with the enhanced visual competence along the retinotectal pathway compared with humans.

sec.title: Molecular similarities of dominant visual pathways within birds and humans
sec.p:
As described before, humans and birds have a distinct dominant visual pathway, corresponding to the retinogeniculate pathway and retinotectal pathway respectively.3 After comparative analyses of the retinotectal pathway between birds and humans, to further reveal the differences between two visual pathways and explore the common characteristics of dominant visual pathways among vertebrates, here we extracted and compared the snRNA-seq data of SC and LG from the human single-cell atlas (Figure 4A).41Figure 4
Two visual pathway comparative analysis
(A) UMAP plot showing the cellular landscape of human SC and LG.
(B) Cells are colored by individuals (left) and brain regions (right).
(C) Heatmap showing the correlation of major cell types between human SC and LG. OPC, oligodendrocyte precursor; c-OPC, committed oligodendrocyte precursor.
(D) Heatmap showing the correlation between avian OT neurons and human visual hubs neurons based on the expression of transcription factors and non-transcription factors.
(E) Venn plot showing the intersection of avian OT upregulated DEGs (blue) and human LG upregulated DEGs (red).
(F) Violin plot showing the expression patterns of selected shared DEGs of avian OT and human LG compared with human SC. ∗∗∗: Wilcoxon rank-sum test p value < 0.001.

Among all major cell types in humans, nerve cells were found to have the most remarkable distinction between LG and SC, especially for the excitatory neurons, possibly reflecting the different visual processing and transmission modes between the two pathways (Figures 4B and S4A). Comparatively, the non-neuron cells, like astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, were more similar between two visual hubs (Figures 4C and S4B). The differential expression analysis further elucidated this characteristic difference of Exn and Inn between human LG and SC (Figure S4C). We found the RNA-editing enzyme ADARB2 and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), including RP11-354K4.2 and NEAT1, were most significantly upregulated in the LG Exn, indicating the influence of RNA regulation in the visual pathway specification. Meanwhile, the LG Inn differentially expressed two long intergenic non-protein coding RNAs, including the LINC02552 and LINC01170, which further underscored the complex transcriptional regulation presented in the retinogeniculate pathway of humans (Figure S4C). Moreover, like the divergence between avian OT (the dominant pathway in birds) and human SC (the subordinate pathway in humans), the differentiated expression patterns of certain functional genes were consistent. For example, the LRRTM4 was downregulated in the subordinate pathway, while CXCL14 was upregulated in all dominant pathways (Figures 3D, 3G, and S4C). Focusing on the upregulated genes in human LG, we found they mainly enriched in functions including the synapse organization and regulation of neuron projection, which was aligned with the dominating information transmission role of the retinogeniculate pathway (Figure S4D).

To explore the relationship between avian OT and different human visual hubs, we included snRNA-seq data of neurons from three key brain regions involved in human visual transmission (SC, LG, and V1), and conducted a correlation analysis with our OT neuron data (Figure 4D). According to previous research reports, the similarity in the expression patterns of transcription factors (TFs) can reflect the developmental homology between brain regions of different species, while other functional genes (like protein-coding genes and lncRNAs) can better manifest the functional similarity and convergence among brain regions.47 Based on the expression of TFs, the Exn and Inn of avian OT were found to be highly similar to the Exn and Inn of human SC, respectively (Figure 4D). This result was expected since OT and SC are broadly known as developmentally homologous brain regions.12 Regarding the expression characteristics of functional genes, the avian OT showed a certain degree of similarity with various human visual functional areas, including the higher-level visual processing center V1, indicating its advanced visual analysis competence in birds. Particularly, the most significant difference between avian OT and human visual hubs was found in the Exn of LG, reflecting substantial differences in the signal transmission patterns of Exn in the human retinogeniculate pathway (Figure 4D).

Despite birds and humans exhibiting differences in their dominant visual pathways, we sought to explore the convergent molecular basis underlying the exceptional visual abilities shared by them. Given the current difficulty in anatomically segmenting the nuclei of the thalamic-retinal pathway in birds, we identified genes highly expressed in avian OT Exn compared to human SC Exn as the dominant visual pathway-enriched genes for birds (Figure S4E). Likewise, we summarized the genes highly expressed in the human LG Exn (dominant pathway) compared to the human SC Exn as well (Figure S4C). The limited number of intersecting genes between the two species further demonstrated the significant transcriptional differences in the Exn of two dominant pathways. Nevertheless, under our filtering conditions, several shared DEGs between two main visual pathways were identified, including 13 commonly upregulated molecules (Figures 4E and 4F; Table S5). Among the genes shared by two dominant visual pathways, half have been proven to play roles in the establishment of visual abilities and neural development. For instance, CDKL5 was reported to be a key gene related to healthy neural development, and individuals lacking its expression will exhibit significant cortical visual impairments.48 The expression of PPFIBP1 is crucial for axon guidance, and its absence can lead to neural development disorders.49 Additionally, ZDHHC14 was revealed to participate in the action potentials of axons and play a role in controlling neuronal excitability.50 Furthermore, CDK6 and NR2F1 are respectively associated with the regulation of cell division and neural development.51,52 GABBR2 is involved in the regulation of Exn receiving signals from Inn and plays a key role in signal processing and transmission.53 Taken together, we found that the majority of genes significantly upregulated in the dominant visual pathway were associated with normal neural development and synapse formation. This molecular consistency may suggest the importance of early developmental processes for the proper formation of visual pathways. Likewise, other unreported genes may also possess similar regulatory potentials in normal neural development. In any case, both these development-related genes and the unreported genes may play a critical role in establishing functional dominant vision, and some of these molecules could potentially serve as markers or targets for early visual neural disorders in the future.

In conclusion, we found that the Exn was the most distinct cell type among visual pathways, both inter-species and cross-species. The transcriptional data highlighted the significant role of specific RNA regulation molecules in the formation of two visual pathways in humans, including RNA-editing enzymes and lncRNAs. Furthermore, the cross-species comparative analysis revealed a series of functional genes associated with the establishment and development of normal vision, which were shared by the dominant visual pathways in both birds and humans, indicating their effects on the visual convergent evolution in vertebrates.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Comparative analysis is a powerful strategy for us to understand brain functions and their evolution across species. Particularly, the innovations and conservations of sensory perception systems are strong showcases for the evolutionary constraints and transformations among vertebrates. Recent technical advances in comparative genetics and single-cell profiling are now providing us with an unprecedented opportunity to identify essential molecules and regulatory mechanisms in complex systems at a more comprehensive and in-depth level.

In this study, we highlighted the significant shift phenomenon of signal transmission weight between two visual pathways in vertebrates and used the snRNA-seq technology to build the first complete cellular landscape of the avian OT. Based on the cellular transcriptome data of representative species on the phylogenetic tree, we conducted three main types of comparative analyses. (1) The comparison of the same visual pathways between different hemispheres in the same species. The avian OT provided us with an ideal model to explore both the oriented projection of visual nerve fibers and hemispheric lateralization. The comparison between the left and right OT identified Exn, Inn, and Ast as the most asymmetric cell types and revealed a series of HEGs, like the EPHA3 and EPHA6, which might play a potential role in the correct extension of retinal ganglion cells. Moreover, leveraging the omics data, we further specified the cell types and brain regions highly expressing these HEGs. (2) The comparison of retinotectal pathways between different species. By integrating snRNA-seq data from the avian OT and human SC, we defined two types of thalamic projecting excitatory neurons with different functional specifications: the vision-related and reflex-related. Their densities presented a significant gradient change from birds to mice and humans. Additionally, we identified a group of neurons with higher density in birds, labeled as Exn5 in this study, highly expressing visual development-related genes. These neurons might contribute to the superior capability of the retinotectal pathway in birds compared to humans. (3) The comparison between two different visual pathways. By comparing the cellular similarity between the human SC and LG, we found that the most remarkable distinction between the two visual hubs exists in nerve cells, especially the Exn. Our analysis provided a list of genes with significant expression differences between the SC and LG, underscoring the importance of RNA regulatory factors such as lncRNAs. Lastly, we identified the conserved upregulated genes in the two dominant pathways of birds and humans. Despite the remarkable dissimilarities between Exn in the retinotectal and retinogeniculate pathways, we found a series of functional genes, like CDK6, CDKL5, and PPFIBP1, consistently highly expressed within the dominant pathway of both birds and humans.

The correct establishment of a visual pathway is essential for various activities in vision-dependent creatures. The comparative analysis and exploration of different visual pathways could help us gain a more comprehensive understanding of our visual perception. Molecules, which play an important role in the formation and transformation of visual pathways, may also be related to the correct vision establishment and visual impairment during individual development. Part of the genes we highlighted in this study has revealed their impact on neurodevelopment and some of them may be used as potential indicators for visual developmental disability in the future. Meanwhile, the systematic exploration of sensory transmission and processing could also provide insights into brain evolution. For instance, the shift in visual weight from the retinotectal pathway to the retinogeniculate pathway in mammals might be closely related to the expansion of the mammalian neocortex, particularly the cephalic shift of higher control centers of the CNS.

In conclusion, in this study, we used the snRNA-seq technology and comparative analysis techniques to decode the cellular and molecular differences in two visual pathways among vertebrates. Particularly, we provided a new roadmap for studying the evolution of neural pathways and underscored the systematic transformation in CNS signal transmission. However, how these molecular and cellular novelties eventually trigger such structural and functional innovations within sensory-associative pathways and brain regions during the evolution of vertebrates still requires more effort to decipher.

sec.title: Limitations of the study
sec.p: The perception and response of complex organisms to the external environment is a highly complicated process. Taking the example of how animals receive light and form visual perception to guide their biological activities, this process involves the collaboration and connection of multiple brain regions, accompanied by intricate transitions of various signal patterns. Our study here mainly focused on the OT structure in birds that received the most retinal projections and performed a preliminary comparison between it and some counterparts in mammals, including the SC, LG, and V1. However, this is just a limited part of visual transmission and processing in vertebrates. Future analyses should incorporate more key hubs of visual perception and processing, encompassing the entire pathway from receiving optical signals at the retina to generating higher-level visual awareness. Additionally, the formation of the visual pathway, particularly for the selective extension of axons, is mainly shaped during the developmental period. However, in this study, we primarily focused on adult samples, which may limit our exploration and results. Lastly, to understand how the vertebrate visual pathway evolved, we should include more species for a more comprehensive comparative analysis. In this study, we identified many differentially expressed genes; however, further efforts are still needed to fully explore a concrete mechanism and establish causation between these genes and visual transformation among vertebrates. Taken together, this research provides a strong foundation for investigating the driving forces behind visual evolution.

sec.title: Experimental model and study participant details
Animal care
sec.p: The animal protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board School, Zhengzhou University (ZZUIRB2022-23). Animal care complied with the guidelines of the local committee. Two pigeons (Columba livia, one male and one female) and two zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata, one male and one female) were used in this study. All birds sampled were healthy adults at 12 months of age. No difference in optic tectum tissue and its cell organization between male and female birds was expected.

sec.title: Sample collection and single-nucleus suspension preparation
sec.p: Adult male zebra finches and pigeons were euthanized and decapitated. The brain was dissected and the optic tectum (OT) sample of the bird was targeted using a specialized hole punch, progressively punched from the periphery to the center to collect the desired tissue sample. All samples were collected separately from each individual and stored independently for subsequent sequencing analysis. For each individual, two independent library replicates were prepared from the OT region. The left and right OT of the pigeons were collected separately, while for the zebra finch, due to the small size of the OT, samples from both hemispheres were combined to ensure sequencing quality here. Samples were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen for subsequent snRNA-seq analysis.

Prepared a single-nucleus suspension following established procedure. Placed the frozen avian brain tissue block in a Dounce homogenizer containing 1 ml of pre-chilled homogenization buffer, and during this process, ensured that the Dounce homogenizer was kept on ice. Homogenized the frozen tissue 10-15 strokes with the loose pestle (pestle A). Then, we filtered the mixture and transferred it to a clean 1-ml Dounce homogenizer. Add 750 μl of homogenization buffer, followed by 10-15 strokes of homogenization with the tight pestle (pestle B). Afterward, the mixture was filtered through a 40 μm filter into a 1.5 ml conical tube, and centrifuged at 500 g for 5 minutes at 4°C to sediment the nuclei. The resulting pellet was resuspended with cell resuspension buffer, and centrifuge again to obtain the final pellet. Finally, resuspend the washed nuclei in the cell resuspension buffer for subsequent preparation of the single-nucleus RNA sequencing library.

sec.title: snRNA-seq library construction and sequencing
sec.p: The DNBelab C high-throughput single-cell library preparation kit (MGI, #1000021082) was utilized to construct the snRNA-seq library following the manufacturer’s instructions. Initially, a single-nucleus suspension was employed for droplet generation. Subsequently, the emulsion was broken, and beads were collected. This was followed by reverse transcription and second-strand synthesis. After that, cDNA amplification and droplet index product amplification were performed to generate a barcoded library. The concentration of the library was measured using the Qubit ssDNA Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #Q10212). Finally, the library was sequenced using the ultra-high-throughput DIPSEQ T1 or DIPSEQ T10 sequencer at the National GeneBank (Shenzhen, China).

sec.title: snRNA-seq raw data processing
sec.p: The sequencing data were processed following the methods previously outlined.56 Initially, bead barcodes and unique molecular identifier sequences were extracted using the ‘parse’ function available in PISA (https://github.com/shiquan/PISA). For cDNA libraries, the first 10–20 base pairs (bp) of ‘read1’ served as bead barcodes, the next 10 bp (21-30 bp) represented the unique molecular identifier (UMI) sequence, and the entire ‘read2’ (100 bp) was employed for downstream alignment analysis. In the case of Droplet Index libraries, the first 10–20 bp of ‘read1’ were designated as bead barcodes, the first 10 bp of ‘read2’ were considered the UMI sequence, and the subsequent 10 bp (11-20 bp) and 10 bp (21-30 bp) of ‘read2’ were designated as droplet index barcodes. Reads with incorrect barcodes, as per the barcode list, were excluded. Subsequently, the single-nucleus RNA-seq data were aligned to the genome reference using STAR (v2.5.3), with the previously modified GTF file.14 To determine the actual number of beads, the ‘barcodeRanks’ function from the DropletUtils tool was utilized to identify the threshold value representing a sharp transition in the distribution of total UMI counts. Beads with UMI counts below this threshold were discarded. Beads considered to belong to the same cell were merged, and gene expression in cells was quantified using PISA.

sec.title: Quality control and clustering of avian snRNA data
sec.p: To reduce the influence of low-quality cells and background noise, we conducted a stringent quality control for our snRNA data of avian OT: (1) First, to remove the ambient RNA of our snRNA data, we applied a R package named SoupX (v1.6.2).57 The cell-specific contamination rate was calculated automatically by SoupX with the raw matrix of each library. All expression matrices were corrected during this step and the adjusted matrices were kept for the following down-stream analyses. (2) After the removal of ambient RNA, we filter low-quality cells with detected genes less than 400 or more than 3,000 or detected counts less than 800. (3) Next, to remove potential doublets in the data, all libraries of the snRNA samples were calculated the doublet score by DoubletFinder (v2.0.3)58 independently with estimated doublet rates (0.8% ∗ cell number). Cells with high doublet scores were removed in this step.

The unsupervised clustering of filtered nuclei of two species was conducted in Seurat (v4.4.0)59 with the same parameters, separately. Before performing dimension reduction and clustering, we merged the processed expression matrices of libraries from the same sample. All expression data were normalized with the function SCTransform() in Seurat. To remove the batch effect between different individuals, we integrated samples by IntegrateData() in Seurat with automatically selected anchors. Then, the non-linear dimension reduction of the integrated object was achieved by function RunUMAP() with resolution=0.8 and dim=1:15. Correspondingly, in this study cells were visualized by the uniform manifold approximation and projection information.

sec.title: Cell type annotation of avian snRNA data
sec.p: Before the cell type annotation, we filtered small clusters with nuclei less than 100 in pigeon and zebra finches. The rest clustered nuclei were annotated by the expression patterns of classic markers for distinct cell types: the excitatory neurons (SLC17A6+), inhibitory neurons (GAD1/GAD2+), oligodendrocytes (PLP1+), astrocytes (SLC1A3/AQP4+), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (PDGFRA+), microglial cells (PTPRC+), blood cells (HBAD+ in zebra finch and A306-00008843RA+ in pigeon) and vascular leptomeningeal cells (COL1A2+). The major cell types were identified in this step. Meanwhile, we manually removed some dissociative clusters or sporadic nuclei that expressed opposite markers of different cell types. Specifically, to obtain a cleaner dataset, here we mainly remove two types of clusters: (1. clusters that do not clearly express any canonical marker genes, labeled as “unknown clusters”. (2. Clusters that co-express markers of both excitatory neurons and interneurons (e.g., SLC17A6/SLC17A7 and GAD1/GAD2). Finally, we obtained 49,273 nuclei for pigeon OT and 28,569 nuclei for zebra finch.

To assess the conservation of cell types within the OT between two bird species and to verify the accuracy of our annotations, we conducted a correlation analysis of cells independently annotated in the OT of the avian species and Bengalese finch. Gene expression data from individuals of both species were normalized using the LogNormalize() function in Seurat (v4.3.0) with default parameters. The top 50 DEGs (p_val_adj<0.05) of each major celltype were selected and retained as parameters for correlation calculation after removing duplicates. The average expression levels of these selected genes in each species were calculated using the AverageExpression() function in Seurat. Subsequently, Spearman correlation analysis was conducted using the psych package (v2.2.5) in R. The p value of Spearman correlation were modified by Holm’s adjustment.

sec.title: The spatial transcriptome data and in situ hybridization results
sec.p: The spatial transcriptome data of pigeon and zebra finch used in this study were in our previous work and publicly available. The expression unit was 100 bins (100 × 100 DNBs,50 mm diameter). The visualization was achieved by the stereo-seq analysis workflow (SAW).60 The in situ hybridization data of zebra finch was retrieved from the ZEBrA database.15

sec.title: Identification of hemisphere-specific expression genes (HEGs)
sec.p: Using the Seurat package’s FindMarkers() function, the differential expression analysis was conducted on major clusters of pigeons, including the Exn, Inn, Oli, Ast, OPC, and VLMC. Parameters ident.1=“L” (left OT), ident.2=“R” (right OT) and min.pct=0.25 were set within the FindMarkers() function. Only those genes with an average fold threshold greater than 0.25 and an adjusted p-value less than 0.05 were included in the HEG statistics. Selected top DEGs with an average fold change greater than 0.5 were displayed in the volcano plot.

sec.title: Processing of human and mouse snRNA-seq data
sec.p: Human snRNA-seq data were annotated based on the original annotation and our unsupervised clustering. Three individuals were all included. For cells annotated as ‘Splatter’ in the original dataset, we split into EXN and INN based on the expression pattern of GAD1 and SLC17A6. Superclusters with cell numbers less than 100 were filtered. The integration between human SC and LG data followed the basic workflow we used in this study and the default pipeline of Seurat. The correlation analysis of major cell types between human LG and SC followed the same workflow as that conducted in the avian dataset. Before visualization, we scaled the Spearman coefficients to highlight the most similar cell types. When counting the sub-class cell type ratio for the integrated object, we used the original sub-class cell type annotated provided by the initial work of this dataset and filtered sub-clusters with cell numbers less than 20. The relative composition of regions for each sub-class cell type was calculated after scaling the total cell number. Any sub-clusters with >80% ratio of certain brain regions were regarded as region-preferred.

For the mouse data, referring to the sample list provided by the original paper, we only selected two dissection regions, including the ‘MB_L2_L2’ and ‘MB_M2_M2’, all of which were tissues from the superior colliculus. We filtered out two individuals which only contained one dissection region and remained the rest four samples for further analysis.

sec.title: Integrated analysis of neurons from humans and birds
sec.p: The neurons from human SC and avian OT were extracted respectively. The genes of birds were transferred into the one-to-one orthologous genes and only genes shared between birds and humans were kept for the integration. All data were split by human and avian individuals and the batch effect between different samples was removed by Seurat. Before the integration, all samples were normalized by the SCTransform() function in Seurat. The integration was based on anchors found by SelectIntegrationFeatures() and achieved by the IntegrateData() function.

sec.title: CABP7+ cell and CBLN2+ cell proportion statistical analysis
sec.p: The proportion of CABP7+ cells was calculated as the percentage of EXN with CABP7 UMI larger than 2 compared with all EXN. For each species, the proportion was calculated in each individual separately. The birds contained four samples, including two pigeons and two zebra finches. The human included three individuals and four individuals were contained for the mouse. The significance test of CABP7+ cell proportion among species was performed with the Kruskal-Wallis test. The same workflow was used for CBLN2+ cell proportion.

sec.title: Relative species proportion for integrated clusters
sec.p: For each cluster of the integrated data between humans and birds, we normalized the cell numbers from each species before the percentage analysis. The cellular composition of each cluster was calculated based on the ratio of humans and birds. We filtered out the Inn10 which contained cells less than 100.

sec.title: Comparative gene ontology enrichment analysis
sec.p: The comparative gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis was conducted on the DEGs (average log2FC>1.0 and adjusted p-value <0.05) of clusters with different species densities, including Exn5, Inn1, and Inn9. DEGs of Exn5, Inn1, and Inn9 were calculated and filtered by the FindAllMarker() function in Seurat. Only DEGs that could be transferred into one-to-one orthologous genes of humans were kept for further analysis. The GO analysis was performed in R using the clusterProfiler package (v4.2.2).61 All genes were converted to ENTREZ IDs using the human genome reference “org.Hs.eg.db”. Comparative GO enrichment was executed by the compareCluster() function with the following parameters: ont=“BP”, pAdjustMethod=“BH”, pvalueCutoff=0.05, and qvalueCutoff=0.05.

sec.title: Correlation between avian OT and human visual hubs
sec.p: Three main human brain regions related to visual pathways were included in this part. We downloaded and processed the human snRNA-seq data as mentioned above. Here, the EXN and INN from human SC, LG, and V1 were used for the correlation analysis with our avian OT data. The data were labeled into six groups by region and cell type, like SC_INN and LG_EXN. We then identified the DEGs among brain regions and their major cell types by the function FindAllMarkers() in the human dataset. The top 50 DEGs (adj_p_value<0.05) of each group were used for the following correlation analysis. The data of avian OT were transferred into one-to-one orthologous genes of humans. Only genes shared between two species were kept. Then the Spearman correlation was conducted in R with package psych (v2.2.5) based on the expression signatures of TF and non-TF genes.

sec.title: Dominant visual pathway common characteristics
sec.p: The DEGs between avian OT_EXN and human SC_EXN were identified by the function FindMarkers() in Seurat with default parameters. Only DEGs with a logarithmic average fold change greater than 0.75 and an adjusted p-value less than 0.05 were regarded as significant. A similar differential analysis was conducted between human LG_EXN and SC_EXN. Up-regulated DEGs shared in the avian OT_EXN and human LG_EXN were highlighted as the common characteristics of two dominant visual pathways.

sec.title: Quantification and statistical analysis
sec.p: No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes, and the sample sizes here are similar to those reported in previous publications. No randomization was used during data collection as there was a single experimental condition for all acquired data. Statistical details of experiments and analyses can be found in the figure legends and main text above. All statistical tests were two-sided, and statistical significance was considered when the p-value <0.05. To account for multiple tests, the p values were adjusted using the Bonferroni correction.
